stimulus.text:
“Without some alteration in our political creed, the superstructure we have been seven years raising at the expence of much blood and treasure, must fall. We are fast verging to anarchy and confusion! . . . Thirteen sovereignties pulling against each other, and all tugging at the Federal head, will soon bring ruin on the whole; whereas a liberal and energetic Constitution, well guarded and closely watched, to prevent encroachments, might restore us to that degree of respectability and consequence, to which we are entitled.”

—George Washington to James Madison, Mount Vernon, November 5, 1786

stem: Which of the following best states Washington's diagnosis of the problem in this letter?

options.text: The states were too weak to defend themselves against Britain
options.misconception: Washington's complaint is about the states pulling against each other, not about weakness against Britain.

options.text: Congress had grown too powerful and was crushing the states
options.misconception: Washington wanted a stronger national government, not a weaker one; Congress under the Articles was feeble.

options.text: Thirteen sovereignties pulling against each other would ruin the Union
The people had lost faith in republican government itself
options.misconception: Washington blames the structure of the government, not the people's faith in republics.

rationales.C: Washington names the disease directly: thirteen sovereignties pulling against each other and tugging at the federal head, which will soon bring ruin on the whole.
rationales.A: The letter blames the states for pulling apart, not Britain for threatening them.
rationales.B: Washington wanted more national power, not less. Background: the Articles Congress was too weak, not too strong.
rationales.D: Washington blames thirteen rival sovereignties, not a loss of faith in republican government.
rationales.general:
1. Washington's image is thirteen sovereignties, each pulling its own way.
2. All of them tug at the federal head, the weak national government.
3. He says that pulling will soon bring ruin on the whole, unless the political creed is altered.
4. Background: under the Articles each state kept its sovereignty, so Congress could only ask, never command.
Remember: when every part pulls its own way, the whole comes apart.
